result:
`index.html` and `poster.svg` are in place and tested at 390px/1440px, with JS disabled, and with reduced motion.

Design-wise, I treated the site as a quiet gallery rather than a shop: a single serif/sans system-font pairing on a warm stone palette, generous whitespace, and no browser chrome-like UI. The vessel occupies a fixed full-viewport layer that stays pinned behind the copy while the hero and the Form/Glaze/Studio chapters scroll over it in normal document flow (alternating left/right panels with a translucent scrim so text is always legible against the object). Scroll position drives a single continuous camera path through four keyframes — an establishing hero view, a raised three-quarter shot for Form, a close dolly on the incised line for Glaze, and a pulled-back elevated angle for Studio — interpolated in three.js using museum-style three-point lighting (no environment map, since `studio.hdr` wasn't delivered) plus a soft shadow-catching plinth. I built a hand-drawn SVG poster (gradient-shaded silhouette with the incised line and a soft ground shadow) as the true default state: it's what renders with JavaScript disabled, and CSS only swaps in the canvas after the scene has proven itself (WebGL context created, module imported, GLTF loaded) — anything short of that, including a fully-failed import, leaves the poster in place with no blank hero or console-visible crash. `prefers-reduced-motion` skips scroll-linked camera movement entirely and shows every chapter fully settled. One thing worth flagging: the vendored `three.module.js` (real r182 build) internally imports a sibling `three.core.js` that split out in recent three.js releases, but that file isn't present anywhere in the kit (confirmed identical across all three build folders, so it's not a one-off copy issue) — meaning true WebGL rendering can never actually succeed with this kit as delivered, and every visit will exercise the "model failing to load" fallback path rather than the live 3D. I left the real three.js integration code in place since it's correct and would work with a complete kit, and made sure the failure is caught silently rather than patched over by fetching the missing file from the internet, which would have violated the "don't reference anything outside this directory" requirement.
